title: Hot days did not lower monthly survival of nine nocturnal desert rodent species at Portal, Arizona, in 1980-2024, although hot days per year tripled (capture-recapture, one site)
abstract: Question: Do daytime heat extremes lower the survival of nocturnal, burrowing desert rodents? Riddell et al. (2021) proposed that burrows protect desert mammals from heat, which explains why mammals stayed stable while desert birds decreased. Approach: We used the Portal Project record (Arizona, Chihuahuan Desert; PortalData 6.122.0, CC0): 26,947 individually marked rodents and 63,638 captures of nine species in 550 monthly (new-moon) intervals from 1980 to 2024, with Daymet daily weather. Cormack-Jolly-Seber models gave apparent monthly survival with free detection for each census, a transient term, season and a 6-month rain anomaly. We added one heat or cold term at a time and inflated standard errors for unexplained time variation. We repeated all fits in 1980-2002 and 2002-2024 and tested the transfer of each term between the periods. Results: Days above the calendar-day 95th percentile of Tmax increased from 10 to 30 per year. The pooled survival effect was +0.008 logit per SD (95% CI -0.034 to +0.051; 1 SD = 2.5 hot days per month); days at or above 38 C gave +0.030 (-0.000 to +0.060), warm nights -0.008 (-0.054 to +0.038). At the lower bound, 20 more hot days per year lower annual survival by at most 3.7%. Surface nesters (harvest mouse, woodrat) did not differ clearly from burrow nesters. Species-level heat effects had both signs and did not predict the other period. Rain had clearer effects (pooled +0.092 per SD in 2002-2024). Detection rose on warm trap nights and fell on rainy nights, so naive return rates gave weather slopes that agreed poorly with survival slopes. Limitations: one site and one weather series; apparent survival includes emigration; no recruitment, breeding or lagged-heat test; Sevilleta and NEON replication data were not downloadable from this host.

Blue: 1980-2024; orange: 1980-2002; green: 2002-2024. Diamonds: random-effects means across species. Heat terms are near zero; rain has the clearest effects.

Portal, Arizona: annual counts of hot days (days above the calendar-day 95th percentile of Tmax, bars; days with Tmax >= 38 C, line) from Daymet V4R1, annual rain, and the number of individual rodents of the nine study species caught per year.

Observation bias. Left: weather slopes of the naive monthly return rate (survival x detection) against CJS survival slopes, per species (95% CI). Right: change in detection with trap-night minimum-temperature anomaly and trap-night rain, from free per-census detection estimates.
